content: An herbalist is an individual whose life is devoted to the economic or medicinal applications of plants. They possess expertise in the harvesting and collection of medicinal plants, a practice often referred to as wildcrafting. A traditional Chinese herbalist is a professional trained or skilled in the preparation and dispensing of herbal prescriptions, functioning as a traditional Chinese herbal medicine practitioner. Similarly, a traditional Ayurvedic herbalist is trained or skilled in the preparation and dispensing of herbal prescriptions within the Ayurvedic medical tradition. An herbalist is also someone trained or skilled in the therapeutic use of medicinal plants. They are professionals educated in herbalism, which involves the use of herbs—also known as botanical or crude medicine—for the treatment of others. Professional designations for herbalists include: Registered Herbalist (RH) from the American Herbalists Guild (AHG). Diplomat in Oriental Medicine from the National Certification Commission for Acupuncture and Oriental Medicine (NCCAOM). Full Member of the National Herbalists Association of Australia (MNHA). Fellow of the National Herbalists Association of Australia (FNHA), a title awarded to Full Members with at least 10 years of membership and clinical practice as an herbalist, along with significant contributions to the profession or the association. Member of the National Institute of Medical Herbalists (MNIMH) or the Irish Institute of Medical Herbalists (MIIMH). The education and training of herbalists vary significantly across different regions of the world. Lay herbalists and practitioners of traditional indigenous medicine often rely on apprenticeships and recognition from their communities rather than formal education. In some countries, formalized training and minimum educational standards exist, though these are not always consistent within or between nations. For instance, in Australia, the profession is currently self-regulated (as of April 2008), leading to different associations setting varying educational standards and recognizing different institutions or training programs. Qualification levels range from diplomas to master’s degrees, with the Advanced Diploma level being regulated to some extent by the national Health Training Packages issued by the Australian National Training Authority. The Course Accreditation System Version 2 of the National Herbalists Association of Australia is widely regarded as the most rigorous and professional standard within the country. Herbalists may engage in the wildcrafting or cultivation of herbs, as well as the diagnosis and treatment of conditions or the dispensing of herbal medications. Most herbal traditions emphasize a constitutional analysis of the client, focusing on treating the patient as a whole rather than merely addressing the disease.
